The '''Bellman filter''' is a recursive algorithm for estimating a sequence of unobserved (latent) states in a [[state-space model]] from noisy observations. It is typically formulated for models with a linear–[[Gaussian state]] transition and a possibly nonlinear and/or non-Gaussian observation density, and it updates the state by solving a per-time-step optimisation problem involving <math>\log p(y_t|x_t)</math>. Under linear–Gaussian observation models, it reduces to the standard [[Kalman filter]] update.<ref name="LangeIntro2024">{{cite arXiv |last=Lange |first=R.-J. |title=Short and simple introduction to Bellman filtering and smoothing |year=2024 |eprint=2405.12668 |class=stat.ME}}</ref><ref name="LangeJoE2024">{{cite journal |last=Lange |first=R.-J. |title=Bellman filtering and smoothing for state–space models |journal=Journal of Econometrics |year=2024 |volume=238 |issue=2 |article-number=105632 |doi=10.1016/j.jeconom.2023.105632|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Kalman1960">{{cite journal |last=Kalman |first=R. E. |title=A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems |journal=Journal of Basic Engineering |year=1960 |volume=82 |issue=1 |pages=35–45 |doi=10.1115/1.3662552}}</ref>

From a dynamic-programming perspective, the Bellman filter applies Bellman's principle of optimality to a mode-estimation problem, yielding a recursion for an (online) maximisation objective whose maximiser is a filtered state estimate. In contrast with grid-based maximisation (as in the [[Viterbi algorithm]] for models with discrete states), the Bellman filter keeps the state space continuous and replaces the exact Bellman value functions by parametric (typically quadratic) ''function-space approximations'', which makes the recursion computationally feasible in moderate to high dimensions. 

== Background ==
In a discrete-time state-space model, an unobserved state vector evolves over time and generates observations. The linear–Gaussian case admits an optimal recursive solution via the Kalman filter, and standard econometric treatments include the monographs by Harvey and by Durbin & Koopman.<ref name="Harvey1990">{{cite book |last=Harvey |first=A. C. |title=Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1990 |isbn=978-0-521-40573-7}}</ref><ref name="DurbinKoopman2012">{{cite book |last=Durbin |first=J. |last2=Koopman |first2=S. J. |title=Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods |edition=2nd |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-19-964117-8}}</ref>

For nonlinear and/or non-Gaussian observation models, exact filtering generally becomes intractable and practical methods rely on approximation (e.g. extended/iterated Kalman filtering) or simulation (e.g. particle filters). The Bellman filter can be presented as a dynamic-programming-based alternative using function-space approximations of the value function at each time step.<ref name="LangeIntro2024" />

== Model and notation ==
Although the approach is more generally applicable, a commonly used specification keeps the classic linear–Gaussian state transition while allowing a general observation density. For <math>t=1,\dots,n</math>:<ref name="LangeIntro2024" />
* '''Observation equation:''' 
<math>y_t \sim p(y_t|x_t)</math>
* '''State-transition equation:'''
<math>
x_t = c + T x_{t-1} + R\eta_t </math>
where <math>\eta_t \sim \text{i.i.d. } \mathcal N(0,Q)</math>.

The filter maintains predicted quantities <math>\hat x_{t\mid t-1}</math>, <math>P_{t\mid t-1}</math> and filtered quantities <math>\hat x_{t\mid t}</math>, <math>P_{t\mid t}</math>.

=== Fisher information ===
For the observation model, [[Fisher information]] is defined as:
<math>
I(x) := \int \left[-\nabla^2 \log p(y|x)\right]\, p(y|x)\,dy,
</math>
where <math>\nabla^2</math> operates on <math>x</math>.
== Algorithm ==
=== Prediction step ===
<math>
\hat x_{t\mid t-1} = c + T\hat x_{t-1\mid t-1},
</math>

<math>
P_{t\mid t-1} = T P_{t-1\mid t-1} T^\top + R Q R^\top.
</math>

This is identical to the prediction step in the Kalman filter.<ref name="Kalman1960"/>

=== Updating step ===
<math>
\hat x_{t\mid t} = \arg\max_{x\in\mathbb R^d}
\left\{
\log p(y_t|x)
-\tfrac12 (x-\hat x_{t\mid t-1})^\top P_{t\mid t-1}^{-1}(x-\hat x_{t\mid t-1})
\right\},</math>

<math>
P_{t\mid t} = \left(P_{t\mid t-1}^{-1} + I(\hat x_{t\mid t})\right)^{-1}.</math>

The update step is well defined if <math>\log p(y_t|x)</math> is concave in <math>x</math> or if <math> P_{t\mid t-1}^{-1}</math> is sufficiently large.<ref name="LangeIntro2024" /><ref name="LangeJoE2024"/> In some cases, <math>I(\hat x_{t\mid t})</math> in the formula for <math>P_{t\mid t}</math> can be replaced by the realised negative Hessian <math>-\nabla^2 \log p(y_t|\hat x_{t\mid t})</math>.

The maximisation can be interpreted as a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of <math>x_t</math>: it combines the log-likelihood term <math>\log p(y_t|x_t)</math> with a quadratic log-prior coming from the Gaussian prediction <math>x_t|y_{1:t-1}\sim\mathcal N(\hat x_{t\mid t-1},P_{t\mid t-1})</math>. Equivalently, the update solves a regularised likelihood problem: it chooses the state that best explains <math>y_t</math> while penalising deviation from the predicted mean <math>\hat x_{t\mid t-1}</math> according to the precision <math>P_{t\mid t-1}^{-1}</math>.

== Special cases and relationships ==
=== Linear–Gaussian observation equation ===
If
<math>
y_t = d + Z x_t + \varepsilon_t </math> 
where <math>
\varepsilon_t \sim \text{i.i.d. } \mathcal N(0,H) </math>,
then the level update <math>
\hat x_{t\mid t} </math> and covariance update <math>
P_{t\mid t}</math> reduce to the usual Kalman filter update.<ref name="LangeIntro2024" /><ref name="LangeJoE2024"/><ref name="Kalman1960" />

=== Iterated (extended) Kalman filtering ===

For a nonlinear observation equation with additive [[Gaussian noise]],
<math>
y_t = h(x_t) + \varepsilon_t,</math> with <math>\varepsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,H)</math>,
the Bellman update objective is proportional to the (negative) nonlinear least-squares criterion
<math>
\tfrac12\,(y_t-h(x))^\top H^{-1}(y_t-h(x))+\tfrac12\,(x-\hat x_{t\mid t-1})^\top P_{t\mid t-1}^{-1}(x-\hat x_{t\mid t-1}).
</math>
Applying a Gauss–Newton method to this problem yields the ''iterated extended Kalman filter'' (see article on the [[Extended Kalman filter|Extended Kalman filter]]). Bell and Cathey show that this iterated update is a Gauss–Newton method for the corresponding maximum-likelihood problem.<ref name="BellCathey1993">{{cite journal
 |last1=Bell |first1=B. M.
 |last2=Cathey |first2=F. W.
 |title=The iterated Kalman filter update as a Gauss–Newton method
 |journal=IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control
 |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=294–297 |year=1993
 |doi=10.1109/9.250476
}}</ref>
Equivalently, this is the special case of the Bellman filter update with <math>\log p(y_t|x)</math> given by the Gaussian log-likelihood <math>-\tfrac12(y_t-h(x))^\top H^{-1}(y_t-h(x))</math> (up to an additive constant).

=== Nonlinear/non-Gaussian state-transition equation===

Although the exposition above assumes a linear–Gaussian state transition (so that the prediction step has closed form), Bellman's recursive approach applies also to state-space models with a general transition density <math>p(x_t|x_{t-1})</math>. In this more general setting, solving Bellman's equation involves a joint maximisation over <math>(x_t,x_{t-1})</math>.<ref name="LangeJoE2024" /> In this setting, degenerate state dynamics can be handled by equating some elements of <math>x_t</math> to those of <math>x_{t-1}</math> and optimising only over the free components.

== Smoothing ==

With a linear–Gaussian state transition, the (fixed-interval) Rauch–Tung–Striebel (RTS) smoother can be applied to the filtered output to obtain smoothed estimates <math>\hat{x}_{t\mid n}</math> and <math>P_{t\mid n}</math>. Define the smoothing gain

<math>
J_t := P_{t\mid t} T^{\top} P_{t+1\mid t}^{-1}.
</math>

Initialise at <math>t=n</math> with <math>\hat{x}_{n\mid n}</math> and <math>P_{n\mid n}</math>. 

Then for <math>t=n-1,\dots,1</math>:

<math>
\hat{x}_{t\mid n} = \hat{x}_{t\mid t} + J_t\bigl(\hat{x}_{t+1\mid n}-\hat{x}_{t+1\mid t}\bigr),
</math>

<math>
P_{t\mid n} = P_{t\mid t} + J_t\bigl(P_{t+1\mid n}-P_{t+1\mid t}\bigr)J_t^{\top}.
</math>

In the Bellman-filter setting (linear–Gaussian state transition with a general observation density), these RTS recursions still apply to the (possibly approximate) filtered quantities produced by the Bellman filter.<ref name="LangeIntro2024" /><ref name="LangeJoE2024"/>

== Parameter estimation ==

In many applications the model depends on unknown static parameters <math>\psi</math> (for example, coefficients in the observation density <math>p(y_t|x_t)</math>, or elements of <math>c,T,R,Q</math>). These can be estimated by fitting <math>\psi</math> to the observed data, typically by running the Bellman filter for each candidate <math>\psi</math> and then maximising an (approximate) log-likelihood objective with a numerical optimiser, subject to any required constraints (e.g. positive definiteness of covariance matrices). A simple estimator of this type is:

<math>
\hat{\psi} := \arg\max_{\psi}\sum_{t=1}^n \left[
\log p\!\left(y_t|\hat{x}_{t\mid t}\right)
-\frac12\log\frac{\det(P_{t\mid t-1})}{\det(P_{t\mid t})}
-\frac12(\hat{x}_{t\mid t}-\hat{x}_{t\mid t-1})^{\top}P_{t\mid t-1}^{-1}(\hat{x}_{t\mid t}-\hat{x}_{t\mid t-1})
\right].
</math>

The first term <math>\log p(y_t|\hat{x}_{t\mid t})</math> measures how well the Bellman-filtered (mode) estimate explains the observation <math>y_t</math>. The remaining terms form a nonnegative regularisation penalty that discourages [[overfitting]] by penalising large adjustments from <math>\hat{x}_{t\mid t-1}</math> to <math>\hat{x}_{t\mid t}</math>, with the determinant ratio reflecting the reduction in (approximate) state uncertainty after incorporating <math>y_t</math>. 

In the linear–Gaussian observation case this coincides with the maximum likelihood estimator; otherwise it can be interpreted as maximising a second-order approximation to the usual prediction-error decomposition.<ref name="LangeIntro2024" /><ref name="LangeJoE2024"/>
